name: Evening math tutor
scenario: A tutor teaches several cohorts using a growing folder of worked examples. The first lesson on a new misconception takes a long time to design; a later adaptation can reuse most of the setup.

tasks.title: Design the first slope clinic
tasks.description: Create an opening diagnostic, two worked examples, and an exit ticket for students who confuse steepness and height.
tasks.details: No previous workshop on this misconception. Need to sketch graphs and try the exit questions myself.

sections.heading: Starting question
sections.body: Give students four small line graphs with the same axes. One line starts high but falls slowly. Another starts low and rises quickly. Ask students to choose the graph with the greater rate of change and explain how they decided.

sections.heading: Misconception to address
sections.body: Several students compared only the final y-values in the entrance exercise. Build an example in which the graph with the larger final value has the smaller positive slope. Keep the intercept visible on both axes.

sections.heading: Deliverables
sections.body: Bring a diagnostic prompt, two annotated examples and a two-item exit ticket. Pair one visual question with one question that uses a short table of values. Include an answer key with a plausible incorrect response.

tasks.title: Adapt the slope clinic for the Tuesday group
tasks.description: Reuse the slope clinic handout, replace the fractions with whole numbers, and shorten it to a 25-minute block.
tasks.details: The graphs, misconception notes and exit ticket already exist. Recheck answers after changing the numbers.

tasks.title: Build the first unit-rate station
tasks.description: Design a hands-on comparison of unit prices for students who divide in the wrong direction. Include an answer key and a quick diagnostic.
tasks.details: No unit-rate handout in the shared folder. Need package-size examples that work without calculators.

tasks.title: Mark the slope exit tickets
tasks.description: Score eight existing short responses and add one feedback line where students compared intercepts.
tasks.details: Use the existing rubric. Students already have the worked examples.

tasks.title: Prepare the next slope practice set
tasks.description: Reuse the worked graph pair, change labels and shuffle the exit ticket for another cohort.
tasks.details: Third time teaching this clinic. Keep the original misconception and answer-key structure.

tasks.title: Reuse the unit-rate station for adults
tasks.description: Update the shopping examples to realistic household sizes and print the existing station cards.
tasks.details: Retain the station instructions and final diagnostic. One example will need a new answer.

tasks.title: Prepare a new scatterplot misconception clinic
tasks.description: Design two contrasting examples for a student who infers causation from a scatterplot. Add an exit question that changes the units.
tasks.details: First time teaching this topic; I have a slide deck but no worked examples or student diagnostic.

tasks.title: Refresh the slope handout for a small group
tasks.description: Take the existing slope clinic and adjust the vocabulary, graph labels and five-minute warm-up.
tasks.details: All four graphs and the diagnostic have already been used successfully in class.

tasks.title: Return the unit-rate quiz
tasks.description: Check twelve quizzes using the existing answer key and identify two questions to review next week.
tasks.details: These are short numeric answers. Add one sample correction for the class.

holdouts.title: Make a shortened slope clinic for revision week
holdouts.description: Trim the saved slope clinic to one graph pair and three practice questions for a mixed revision group.
holdouts.details: Use the final April version. Keep the exit question and the existing answer key; only two numerical labels change.
holdouts.check: Tests whether repeated reuse/familiarity limits the influence of the first expensive slope lesson. The estimator need not implement an explicit time trend.

holdouts.title: Design a first lesson about repeated chance trials
holdouts.description: Prepare two contrasting examples, a short sorting activity, and an exit ticket about a new misconception.
holdouts.details: I have not taught this topic before. The class has done simple probability, and I have the attached exit-slip notes.

pdf.title: Clinic request: after a string of heads

sections.heading: From exit slips
sections.body: Several students said a tail is due after three heads. Two argued that a six is less likely because a die had just rolled two sixes. Students can already count outcomes for one fair die.

sections.heading: Lesson scope
sections.body: Use one coin sequence and one die sequence. Decide where students will predict before observing a result and where they will explain the independence assumption. Avoid a long simulation that would use the entire session.

sections.heading: Materials requested
sections.body: Prepare a two-column card sort, two worked examples with contrasting explanations, and an exit question that changes the object being tossed. Provide a short key suitable for another tutor to use.

holdouts.check: Tests whether a new topic with no reusable handout is matched to other first-time lesson designs despite the many quick adaptations in the same category.
